What happens when 50 concurrent users attempt to book the exact same VIP shuttle seat at the exact same millisecond?
Double-booking? Frozen UI? Or a silent data race?
Most reservation systems look great in staging, but crumble under high-concurrency race conditions during peak flash sales.
In my latest architectural prototype, TransFlow AI — an executive intercity shuttle reservation platform for the Bandung – Jakarta corridor — I explored a resilient, production-grade architecture leveraging Feature-Sliced Design (FSD), Optimistic UI rollback mechanisms, and action-oriented AI via Model Context Protocol (MCP):
1️⃣ Optimistic UI with Instant Conflict Rollback:
Delivers instant 0ms perceived latency for passengers selecting seats. If a backend collision occurs (HTTP 409 Conflict), the UI immediately rolls back to its previous snapshot and gracefully marks the contested seat as held by another session—without breaking the user flow.
2️⃣ Anti-Race Distributed Atomic Lock:
Guarantees zero double-booking risk by securing seats through atomic locks with a 600-second (10-minute) TTL. Built-in stress test simulator executes 50 parallel bot threads competing for high-demand seats in real-time.
3️⃣ Action-Oriented AI via Model Context Protocol (MCP):
The AI Concierge isn’t just a passive conversational bot. Through MCP tools, it acts as an autonomous operational copilot:
• Queries real-time tollway sensors (`get_corridor_telemetry`) to monitor weather radar and traffic bottlenecks along the Cipularang expressway.
• Dynamically calculates estimated arrival times (`calculate_dynamic_eta`).
• Grounded RAG with real physical constraints: The Toyota HiAce Premio stands at 2.28m, strictly barring it from entering the elevated MBZ tollway (2.10m clearance gantry)—enforcing routing through the lower expressway for structural safety.
4️⃣ Authentic Top-Down Automotive Blueprint:
A precision cabin blueprint reflecting Indonesian automotive ergonomics: Right-Hand Drive (RHD) cockpit, curbside electric sliding door, and a distinct separation between 100% Flat Floor seats (Rows 1 & 2) vs. Rear Wheel Well arch protrusions (Row 3).
🛠️ Tech Stack: Next.js 15 (App Router), TypeScript, Feature-Sliced Design (FSD), Tailwind CSS, Model Context Protocol (MCP), Vector RAG, and jsPDF.

Over the past few months I've been building VenHub (Vendor Hub), an operations portal for vendors and internal teams at iForte Solusi Infotek. Field surveys and FTTH preventive maintenance used to run through many manual steps across several systems. VenHub moves that flow into one portal connected directly to Salesforce.

What VenHub does today: 
1. Connectivity Survey Salesforce sends surveys to vendors. Vendors fill in the Survey Form section by section, with photos per group. After submission, Salesforce creates or updates the Work Report and sends the status (Submitted, Approved or Rejected) back to VenHub.
2. Automatic PHS documents When a survey is Approved, the system calculates quantities against the PHS price list, generates the PDF, and uploads it to the Work Report in Salesforce. Failed deliveries retry automatically and can also be resent manually.
3. FTTH Preventive Maintenance Technicians submit a Customer ID, a category, and evidence photos. The photo count is validated against the category. Salesforce then sends the Work Order and Service Appointment status back.

What's next We plan to move more of the FTTH business process into VenHub, so vendors and internal teams work from one place.

Security and personal data protection VenHub holds customer and vendor data, so I built this in from the start, using Indonesia's Personal Data Protection Law (UU PDP) as the reference:
1. Email OTP login, plus mandatory Microsoft Authenticator for Super Admins and Admins
2. Temporary account lock after repeated failed logins, and automatic logout when idle
3. Personal data masked in logs and in views for roles that shouldn't see it
4. Access to personal data recorded: who, which role, which endpoint
5. Automatic data retention for logs, histories and notifications

Tech stack:
1. Backend: Go (Gin), PostgreSQL, JWT, TOTP
2. Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn/ui, Zustand, React Hook Form + Zod, acting as a BFF so the browser never handles the API token
3. Integrations: Salesforce (Apex/LWC and REST), internal email service
4. Deployment: Docker & Jenkins

What I learned:
1. Two-way integration needs retries, idempotency, and clear logs, or small failures are hard to trace.
2. Security and privacy cost far less when built in from the beginning.
3. As developers, we have to solve problems, keep learning, and adapt to whatever comes up. We shouldn't idolize a single platform, because a developer needs to see the big picture and pick the tools that will actually help the company.

Thanks to the team who helped along the way Andrey Sholinka, Dwiky Kurniawan, Daffa Asyqar Ahmad Khalisheka, Karina Virgi, Viriya Putta, Jessica Jetje Joanna.

"Will the Nvidia fallout kill off Asia’s data centre boom?
Projects that touted chip access to Chinese customers face tighter US scrutiny

After #JensenHuang’s abrupt return to the helm of Nvidia, big questions still loom over south-east Asia’s data centres, which have benefited from voracious demand for top-end AI chips but face tougher US export rules.

Countries such as Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia have received hundreds of billions of dollars of #investment from tech giants and#datacentre developers, as the region becomes one of the fastest-growing hubs for#AI infrastructure.

But new restrictions from Washington this month aimed at closing a loophole that allowed Chinese companies to use American#chips in south-east Asian data centres have put much of that investment in jeopardy.

The new rules — which were announced as US authorities investigate Singaporean business Megaspeed over alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips to China — have the potential to cause legal complications, financing issues and due diligence concerns for hundreds of projects under development.

The financial implications are far-reaching. Banks,#privateequity firms, creditors and tech groups have committed billions of dollars to the projects, which have attracted Chinese customers such as#TikTok owner ByteDance and Alibaba.

The new rules, which came into effect last Thursday, require data centre operators in five countries — Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil — that supply significant processing power to Chinese customers to obtain special licences from the US government to buy advanced American chips.

Washington is expected to assess which Chinese companies will have access to the chips and then decide whether to grant the licences based on how they plan to use the computing power. Operators have 90 days to obtain the licences.

Analysts expect the US to reject companies that plan to use chips to train large language models, as Washington seeks to slow down Beijing in the AI race."

For decades, we've followed a familiar approach to construction.

Bring the materials to the site.

Arrange the labour.

Build everything from the ground up.

And manage the challenges that come along the way.

But I've often wondered.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗱𝗼 𝘄𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘂𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝘀𝗼 𝗺𝘂𝗰𝗵 𝗼𝗳 𝗮 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝗶𝘁𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳?

When I first explored prefabricated construction in Indonesia, one thing caught my attention.

The possibility of completing a significant part of the construction process before the materials even reach the site.

Instead of starting everything from scratch, structural components can be manufactured in a controlled environment.

Measurements are planned.

Materials are prepared with precision.

Quality can be monitored throughout production.

And once the components reach the site, the focus shifts from extensive construction to systematic assembly.

This approach changes more than just the construction timeline.

It can help reduce material wastage, improve consistency, and minimise dependence on unpredictable site conditions.

Of course, not every building can or should be manufactured entirely in a factory.

Site preparation, foundations, installation, and skilled workmanship will always remain important.

But I believe the balance between factory work and on-site construction will continue to evolve.

At Techle Indo Innovation, we've been exploring this approach through prefabricated wooden cottages and modular building systems.

And the more I understand its possibilities, the stronger my belief becomes.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀𝗻'𝘁 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗲.

𝗜𝘁'𝘀 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝗼𝗻-𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝗿, 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗲𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝘁, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗱.

Perhaps the next big transformation in #construction won't take place at a construction site.

It will begin on a factory floor.

Two industrial sites. An international collaboration. A valuable chapter in my journey as an energy engineer.

Through PT Langgeng Ciptalindo, I had the opportunity to participate in the Indonesia–Denmark Energy Partnership Programme (INDODEPP), involving the Embassy of Denmark in Indonesia and ASEAN, the Danish Energy Agency, and Viegand Maagøe.

The initiative provided grant support for energy audits across 12 industrial facilities. My involvement covered two of them: PT Laju Perdana Indah and PT Sorini Agro Asia Corporindo (Cargill).

Much of my work centred on boilers: examining operating data, assessing energy performance, and working with the team to identify improvement opportunities. Discussions with plant personnel were an essential part of the process, helping us connect the numbers with actual operating conditions.

The work continued beyond the site visits. I contributed to the overall energy audit reports and Investment Summary Reports, bringing together findings to support the evaluation of potential energy efficiency investments.

This part of the experience changed how I viewed an audit recommendation. A technically sound idea needs a clear explanation of its potential savings, investment requirements, and operational implications so that the people responsible can assess its value.

I came away with stronger technical skills and a greater appreciation for the collaboration behind a useful energy audit. Plant teams, auditors, and international partners each brought perspectives that helped shape the assessment.

Thank you to our partners, the teams at both facilities, and my colleagues at PT Langgeng Ciptalindo for the opportunity to contribute and learn. I look forward to carrying these lessons into future work in industrial energy efficiency.

Indonesia's AI opportunity is much bigger than chatbots.

Most of the conversation is about using AI. The bigger economic prize is building the industry behind it.
 
The scale is real. According to the e-Conomy SEA 2026 report by Google, Temasek and Bain, Indonesia's digital economy is projected to reach US$119 billion in GMV this year, up 16% year-on-year. The government has also cited an estimate that AI could contribute around US$366 billion to Indonesia's GDP by 2030.
 
These are projections, not guaranteed outcomes. And they raise a harder question:
 
How much of this value will Indonesian companies actually capture?
 
A large AI market does not automatically make us an AI industry. That requires capability across the value chain:
 
1. Infrastructure: data centres, GPU computing, sovereign cloud and reliable energy.
2. Platforms: local AI models, data engineering, MLOps and system integration.
3. Solutions: AI for banking, energy, manufacturing, healthcare and government.
4. Security & Governance: AI risk assessment, data protection, model security and continuous monitoring.
5. Talent: AI engineers, data scientists, cybersecurity and AI governance professionals.
 
Infrastructure attracts the headlines and the capital. The more durable opportunity lies in the capabilities to build, integrate, operate and secure the ecosystem.
 
The same report shows why. Indonesia has the largest generative AI user base in Southeast Asia, around 105 million people. Yet our depth of AI usage is the lowest among the SEA-6 markets.
 
We have the scale. The task now is to turn adoption into productivity, innovation and domestic value creation.
 
One layer deserves particular attention. AI without cybersecurity is an expensive experiment waiting for its first incident. As adoption accelerates, so do the risks: data exposure, model manipulation, identity abuse and AI-enabled attacks.
 
This is where ITSEC Asia aims to contribute: helping organisations adopt and secure AI responsibly, and developing cyber and AI talent through ITSEC Cyber & AI Academy.
 
The ambition should go beyond deploying someone else's technology. Indonesia should not only be the market for the AI revolution. We should be one of its builders.

Where should Indonesia focus first: AI infrastructure, local AI innovation, security, or talent?
